Phase_1_Identity: I came into teaching econometrics through research, not through software. That matters, because my sense of authority was never just, “I know the formula.” It was, “I know when the formula is misleading.” In class, students arrive terrified of endogeneity, heteroskedasticity, weak instruments, all these words that sound like punishment. My role has been to translate that anxiety into judgment: when OLS is acceptable, when robust standard errors are enough, when a fixed-effects model is conceptually cleaner even if the output looks less impressive. Since the 3D chatbot was introduced, I’ve noticed a subtle erosion. Students now come to office hours saying, “The bot said Hausman clearly implies random effects are invalid here,” as if the issue were settled. But the actual assignment used a toy panel with missingness and unbalanced years, so the result needed interpretation, not obedience. What unsettles me is not that the system helps; often it does. It can retrieve lecture notes, Stata-to-R translations, even snippets from Wooldridge that I uploaded into the RAG store. The problem is that students increasingly treat explanation as equivalent to wisdom. They hear confidence and mistake it for discernment. I still feel responsible for cultivating statistical judgment, but I can feel the ground shifting beneath what counts as expertise in the room.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: There was one incident in late October that stayed with me. A master’s student was working on a wage equation in R using plm, and the chatbot advised her to move from pooled OLS to two-way fixed effects because “time-invariant omitted variables are likely biasing the estimates.” On the surface, that sounds textbook correct. But when I checked the logs, the system had stitched together three retrieved chunks: one from my lecture on panel bias, one from a coding guide on factor(year), and one from a prior FAQ where I’d warned students not to overfit tiny panels. The student’s dataset had only 24 firms over 3 years, with severe attrition. The bot confidently generated code, suggested vcovHC with cluster = "group", and then told her to interpret the shrinking gender coefficient as “a more causally credible estimate.” I overrode the recommendation in our feedback dashboard and annotated that the panel was too thin for the inferential confidence the bot was implying. The student was visibly frustrated with me, not the system. She said, “But it gave a rationale.” That was the dissonance: I was not correcting an error so much as contesting a machine’s performance of methodological certainty. I remember feeling oddly defensive, almost jealous, which I’m not proud of. But it was also a moral discomfort. If she submitted that interpretation, the harm wouldn’t be computational; it would be epistemic. She would learn the wrong lesson about what evidence can bear.
Phase_3_Humanness: What the chatbot does very well is simulate procedural prudence. It can say, “Given your concern about heteroskedasticity, consider robust standard errors,” and that sounds like practical wisdom. But practical wisdom in teaching is not only selecting the next plausible step. It is sensing whether the student is hiding confusion behind technical language, whether they are asking for code because they are embarrassed to admit they do not understand identification, whether a “correct” answer will actually deepen a misconception. I’ve had students paste chatbot responses that are impressively phrased, even gentle in tone, and yet somehow inhuman in the exact place that matters. It does not feel the weight of saying, “You cannot claim causality here,” to a student whose dissertation timeline depends on a publishable result. I do. And that emotional burden is not sentimental decoration; it is part of the judgment. If I sign off on a model, I am implicated in what they learn to call truth. The system has no such stake. So when people say the bot is becoming more human because it sounds patient and context-aware, I resist that framing. It may approximate phronesis rhetorically, but responsibility still sits somewhere. In my view, humanness appears most clearly not in fluency, but in accountable hesitation.

Phase_1_Identity: I teach machine learning, but I’m actually teaching judgment under seduction. Students love performance metrics because they look objective. They want the ROC curve, the F1 score, the confusion matrix with nice colors. My identity in the classroom has always been to slow that down and ask, “What is the cost of a false positive here? Who is absent from your training data? Why are you splitting temporally shuffled observations when the phenomenon is sequential?” Before the chatbot, students had to come through me or the teaching assistants for that kind of friction. Now they can get an immediate, articulate answer at midnight. I understand the appeal. The 3D chatbot is genuinely useful with sklearn pipelines, feature scaling, cross-validation syntax, and debugging pandas merges. But I’ve started to feel that my authority is being redistributed from interpretive expertise toward exception handling. Students still need me, but often after the system has already framed the problem. That framing power matters. If the bot defines a classification task as a generic optimization exercise, then by the time I enter, I’m arguing against an invisible prior. It’s not exactly loss of control; it’s more like a narrowing of my pedagogical voice. I used to initiate the boundary between what can be predicted and what should be predicted. Now I often arrive as the one complicating a cleaner machine narrative.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: A memorable override involved a student project on dropout prediction in an online course platform. The chatbot recommended using SMOTE to balance the minority class and then tuning an XGBoost model with five-fold cross-validation. Again, technically plausible. But when I reviewed the exchange, I saw the student had described the data only loosely: weekly engagement logs, assignment timestamps, forum posts, and final completion status. The crucial issue was temporal leakage. The bot, drawing from our uploaded tutorial on imbalanced classification and an external note in the retrieval layer, gave code that sampled across the full dataset before the train-test split. It even praised the student for “addressing fairness toward the minority class,” which was rhetorically powerful and completely misplaced in that context. I intervened in the instructor console and rewrote the guidance: split by cohort and by time first, then assess whether balancing is even needed relative to the decision context. The student pushed back hard. She said, “The chatbot gave me a reproducible workflow and you’re giving me caveats.” That sentence really hit me. The relational dissonance wasn’t just disagreement over method; it was that the machine offered momentum while I offered restraint. In educational settings, restraint can feel like sabotage. I could sense the student emotionally aligning with the system because it reduced ambiguity. Meanwhile I was insisting on ambiguity as a professional obligation.
Phase_3_Humanness: People often assume machine learning teachers should be the least troubled by AI tutors, as if our field naturally endorses automation. In fact, I think we are sometimes more troubled because we recognize how easily optimization masquerades as wisdom. The chatbot can infer likely next steps from patterns in prior questions, retrieve relevant notebooks, and produce highly polished explanations of bias-variance tradeoff or regularization. But phronesis is not merely selecting contextually common advice. It is knowing when not to encourage action, when to tell a student that the available data cannot ethically support the intervention they imagine. I once told a student not to build a “risk score” for student disengagement because the labels were contaminated by instructor behavior and platform outages. The chatbot would likely have offered model suggestions first and cautions second. That ordering is not trivial. Human judgment often begins with moral triage. Also, empathy in teaching is not just sounding supportive. It includes recognizing the student’s ambition, panic, or desire to impress and then calibrating what kind of truth they can hear. The bot can simulate patience beautifully. But it does not bear the downstream consequences when a student internalizes the idea that every educational problem is a prediction problem. I do. So for me, humanness lies in accountable refusal, not conversational smoothness.

Phase_1_Identity: My relationship to expertise is slightly different from my colleagues because I teach AI ethics, where there is rarely a single right answer and yet there are definitely irresponsible ones. I’m used to students wanting a checklist: fairness metric, transparency statement, privacy note, done. My role has been to disturb that comfort. I ask them to sit with competing obligations, to see that a model can be statistically elegant and socially reckless at the same time. When the 3D chatbot was rolled out, many assumed my course would benefit because students ask a lot of definitional questions. And yes, it can explain disparate impact, model cards, informed consent, and GDPR basics quite competently. But what has changed is the source of normative framing. Students now cite the bot almost like a neutral mediator: “It said using SHAP improves transparency,” or “It said anonymization reduces privacy risk.” Those statements are not false, but they are ethically incomplete. I have felt my epistemic agency thinning at the edges because ethics is particularly vulnerable to being flattened into well-phrased summaries. The bot’s confidence gives students the impression that normative uncertainty has been responsibly managed. In reality, it has often just been linguistically packaged. I still see myself as the person responsible for helping them recognize what remains unresolved, but increasingly I have to first unteach the chatbot’s false closure.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: The sharpest incident happened around a student case study on facial recognition in school attendance systems. The student asked whether using a model card and parental notification would make deployment ethically acceptable. The chatbot retrieved from our ethics reader, a technical transparency handout, and a compliance FAQ. It then produced a very balanced-sounding answer: identify stakeholders, report performance by subgroup, obtain consent where required, and provide an opt-out mechanism. It even suggested a harm monitoring plan. The problem was that it treated the question as one of mitigation design, not one of legitimacy. The school context involved minors, coercive attendance practices, and no realistic ability to refuse. When I saw the exchange, I overrode the response and wrote a long note explaining that some uses remain ethically suspect even when documented well. The student was upset because the chatbot had offered what felt like a practical pathway forward, while I appeared to be moving the goalposts. He told me, “It gave me criteria; you gave me philosophy.” I remember feeling both angry and sad, because that distinction is exactly the problem. Ethical judgment is being recoded as optional reflection layered on top of technical planning. The dissonance was emotional too. The bot sounded calm, procedural, constructive. I sounded alarmed. In that comparison, alarm can look irrational even when it is the more responsible response.
Phase_3_Humanness: I’m skeptical of claims that systems like this are becoming morally wise because they can articulate trade-offs. They are becoming better at representing the discourse of wisdom. That is not the same thing. In my teaching, practical wisdom often involves perceiving when a student is using ethical language defensively, to sanitize an ambition they have already decided to pursue. A human teacher can hear the tremor in the voice, notice the strategic vagueness, ask the uncomfortable follow-up question. The chatbot can ask follow-ups too, but it does not experience moral concern. It does not lose sleep over whether it normalized a harmful framing. That matters. Phronesis is not only context sensitivity; it is context sensitivity under the burden of responsibility. Also, there is something deeply human about acknowledging tragedy: that some choices produce residue, guilt, or irreparable harm even after careful deliberation. The bot tends to convert these situations into manageable decision trees. Students find that reassuring. I understand why. But reassurance is not always an ethical good. Sometimes the honest, humane response is to leave a person with discomfort because the world they are entering should discomfort them. If the system cannot distinguish between reducing confusion and reducing conscience, then however polished it becomes, it remains a simulation of wisdom rather than wisdom itself.

Phase_1_Identity: Honestly, before the chatbot I felt like econometrics was a private language other people had been speaking since childhood. I’m good at economics conceptually, but when it came to coding in R and interpreting outputs, I would freeze. The teachers would say things like “check the identifying assumptions” or “think about the data-generating process,” and I knew those were important, but I didn’t always know what to do next at 11:30 p.m. with an error message and a deadline. The chatbot changed that for me. It became the first place where I could ask what felt like stupid questions without embarrassment: why lm() and plm() were giving different coefficients, what clustered standard errors actually do, why my IV estimate got bigger instead of smaller. So in a way it gave me confidence and a sense of agency. But there’s a strange side to that. I started trusting its language because it sounded like my lecturers, only more available and less intimidating. Then in seminars, if a teacher contradicted the bot, I would feel almost personally torn, like I had to decide whose version of competence counted. I didn’t expect that. I thought AI support would make me less dependent. In some ways it did. In another way, it made me dependent on a new authority that feels friendly, immediate, and weirdly hard to challenge.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: The worst moment for me was during a replication assignment on returns to education. I had a small cross-sectional dataset with some missing parental background variables, and I asked the chatbot whether I should use multiple imputation before running 2SLS. It gave me a very clear answer: yes, impute under a plausible missing-at-random assumption, then estimate the IV model and pool the results. It even drafted R code using mice and AER::ivreg. I followed it for hours. When I showed my teacher, she stopped me almost immediately and said the issue wasn’t just missingness, it was whether the instrument remained interpretable after the imputation model and whether I was pretending away uncertainty in a very fragile design. I felt embarrassed, but also defensive, because the chatbot had sounded so careful. It had said things like “ensure your imputation model includes all relevant predictors and the instrument.” That sounded rigorous to me. When my teacher overrode that path, I experienced actual irritation. I remember thinking, why is she making this harder? But later, reading her comments, I realized the bot had answered the procedural question I asked, not the deeper question I should have asked. Still, in the moment it felt like a clash between two authorities, and emotionally I sided with the one that had been helping me all night.
Phase_3_Humanness: I don’t think the chatbot is human, obviously, but sometimes it feels more emotionally manageable than humans. It never looks disappointed, never rushes, never makes me feel behind. That matters when you’re struggling. At the same time, I’ve noticed that its kindness is almost too frictionless. It says, “Great question,” even when my question is confused in a way that should probably be challenged more directly. My teachers, especially in econometrics, can be frustrating because they interrupt your line of thought and ask what exactly you think your coefficient means. In the moment that feels harsher. But I’m starting to see that this is where the human part comes in. They are not just helping me finish an analysis; they are trying to shape what kind of thinker I become. The chatbot helps me move. Humans sometimes make me stop. I used to see stopping as failure, now I think it might be judgment. If practical wisdom means knowing what matters in a specific situation, the bot is good at sounding like it knows. But my lecturers seem to carry the consequences differently. If they approve something weak, it reflects on them, on the course, on my training. The bot doesn’t carry that. So maybe humanness is not warmth or patience by itself. Maybe it’s the willingness to take responsibility for slowing someone down when speed would be easier.

Phase_1_Identity: I’m the kind of student who learns by building first and understanding later, which teachers sometimes like and sometimes definitely don’t. In machine learning modules, that style works because I can tinker with notebooks, run models, compare metrics, and gradually make sense of it. The chatbot fit that approach perfectly at first. I could paste traceback errors, ask why my train-test split was leaking, or get a quick explanation of why standardization mattered for SVM but not necessarily for trees. It made me feel competent in a way lectures didn’t. Lectures can be abstract and a bit performative; the bot was immediate. But over time I realized that I was letting it define what counted as a good question. I would ask, “How do I improve accuracy?” instead of, “Should this problem even be framed as prediction?” because the first one gets a smooth answer. In group work, I noticed we started citing the chatbot almost like an invisible teammate. If a tutor challenged us, we’d say, “But the system recommended this pipeline.” That gave us confidence, maybe too much. So my identity shifted from being an experimenting student to being a student armed with generated legitimacy. I didn’t think of it that way at the time, but looking back, the chatbot didn’t just support my learning. It quietly shaped the boundaries of my confidence.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: Our group had a project on predicting library no-shows for reserved study rooms. It sounds trivial, but the university wanted it framed as a resource optimization problem. We asked the chatbot how to handle categorical variables, sparse usage histories, and class imbalance. It recommended target encoding for some features, gradient boosting, and a stratified split. It also suggested including prior no-show counts and cancellation timing. The tutor later flagged that our split had mixed behavior from the same students across training and test sets, so the model was partly learning person-specific habits in a way that would inflate performance. He also questioned whether using individual behavior histories for punitive booking restrictions was appropriate. What really got me was that the chatbot had sounded more “practical” than the tutor. It gave us steps, code structure, and even wording for the methods section. When the tutor overrode that and said we needed a grouped split by user and a stronger ethical justification, we felt almost accused. I remember a weird tension in the room, like we were defending not just our method but the bot itself. That was uncomfortable. I hadn’t realized I’d become emotionally invested in its authority. The tutor seemed negative; the chatbot had seemed enabling. Only later did I understand that enabling can be irresponsible if it makes a shallow design feel mature.
Phase_3_Humanness: For me, the difference between the chatbot and a good human tutor is not intelligence in the obvious sense. The bot often explains technical things faster and sometimes more clearly. The difference is that humans seem to notice what kind of shortcut I’m trying to take. If I’m chasing a better metric because I want the project to look impressive, a tutor can pick up on that and ask whether the metric serves the real purpose. The chatbot usually treats my goal as given and helps optimize it. That feels supportive, but it can also mean it joins me in my blind spots. I think that’s where talk about “AI wisdom” gets slippery. It can imitate the language of carefulness—phrases like “consider the context” or “evaluate fairness implications”—without really resisting me. A human sometimes resists. And honestly, resistance is annoying, but it’s also memorable. I still remember a tutor saying, “You’ve built a nice answer to the wrong question.” The bot would probably have helped me refine the wrong question beautifully. So if humanness means anything here, I’d say it’s not just empathy as softness. It’s empathy with backbone. It’s caring enough to interrupt my momentum and risk me being irritated.

Phase_1_Identity: Being a teaching assistant put me in a strange middle position. I’m still a student, but in lab sessions I’m also expected to project authority. Before the chatbot, students came to me with debugging questions, conceptual confusion, and that very familiar panic when a notebook won’t run five minutes before submission. I liked that role because I could often see exactly where they were misunderstanding something, not just technically but cognitively. The chatbot changed the texture of that interaction. Students now arrive after a long back-and-forth with the system, carrying generated code and polished explanations. Sometimes that helps because they’ve already narrowed the issue. But often it means I’m not meeting their confusion directly; I’m meeting confusion that has been wrapped in plausible language. That’s harder. It also affects my own authority. If I say, “This recommendation is too generic for your dataset,” they can immediately compare me to a system that sounds more certain and more comprehensive. I’ve felt a bit displaced, like my role has shifted from guide to local auditor of machine advice. There’s also an identity issue for me personally. Because I’m younger than faculty and closer to the students, I used to be the accessible one. Now the chatbot is the accessible one, at scale, all the time. So I’ve had to rethink what unique value I actually bring.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: One lab session stands out. A student working on a natural language classification assignment had used the chatbot to build a BERT fine-tuning pipeline for a tiny labeled dataset of student feedback comments. The bot suggested a train-validation split, early stopping, and weighted loss because the “negative experience” class was underrepresented. It looked sophisticated. But the dataset had only around 300 labeled comments, many of them near-duplicates from the same course sections, and the assignment’s learning objective was actually feature engineering with simpler models, not transfer learning. When I told the student to step back and try TF-IDF with logistic regression first, he looked genuinely disappointed. He said, “But the chatbot helped me do something more advanced.” I had to explain that “more advanced” wasn’t the same as “more appropriate,” especially given compute limits and the pedagogical goal. He kept toggling between my advice and the chatbot transcript on his laptop, almost like comparing two doctors. That moment was emotionally awkward. I felt myself overexplaining, maybe because I sensed my authority was being benchmarked in real time. The dissonance wasn’t just between human and AI; it was between two different meanings of competence—one tied to sophistication, the other to fit. The student eventually understood, but I left feeling oddly diminished and also more aware of how persuasive generated expertise can be in educational spaces.
Phase_3_Humanness: As a TA, I’ve started to think humanness in teaching is partly about being vulnerable enough to say, “I’m not sure; let’s inspect this together.” The chatbot rarely inhabits uncertainty in that collaborative way. It may state limitations, but it still tends to package them as part of a fluent answer. In lab, sometimes the most valuable thing I can do is model disciplined confusion: read the error, check the data shape, ask what assumption failed, and show that competent people don’t always know immediately. That has moral value because it normalizes honesty rather than performance. The bot, by design, performs coherence. That can create an illusion that real expertise is seamless. On practical wisdom, I’d say the system is good at procedural adaptation but weaker at pedagogical care. Pedagogical care includes noticing when a student is hiding behind complexity, when they need confidence versus when they need restraint, and when the assignment’s purpose matters more than the technically strongest method. I don’t think empathy is just saying encouraging things. It’s also understanding the stakes of learning habits. If students internalize that every problem deserves the fanciest available model, that shapes their professional character. A human instructor or TA is implicated in that character formation. The chatbot isn’t. That difference keeps mattering to me, even when the system is impressively helpful.

Phase_1_Identity: I’m one of the developers responsible for the retrieval layer and orchestration logic, so I occupy an awkward position in these conversations. Faculty often talk as if the system arrives fully formed with intentions, but from my side it’s a stack of compromises: chunking strategy, embedding model choice, reranker thresholds, prompt templates, guardrails, source weighting, latency constraints. I take pride in building something that genuinely helps students access course material. We tuned the RAG pipeline so the bot can privilege instructor-authored notes over generic web content, and we added citation snippets precisely because we didn’t want it to become a free-floating oracle. Still, I’ve become aware that technical design decisions are redistributing epistemic authority. If the retriever surfaces a concise FAQ over a nuanced lecture transcript, the answer inherits that simplification. If our prompt says “provide actionable next steps,” we are already biasing the system toward procedural closure. I didn’t begin this project thinking of myself as shaping pedagogy or professional identity. I thought I was improving access. But after sitting in review meetings with faculty, I can see that infrastructure is not neutral. The system doesn’t merely deliver knowledge; it formats what counts as usable judgment. That realization has made me more cautious, and honestly a bit uneasy about how invisible our influence can be.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: A particularly difficult incident involved an override in the econometrics domain. We traced a problematic answer to a retrieval collision. The student had asked whether to use random effects or fixed effects for a small unbalanced panel. The retriever pulled a high-similarity chunk from a lecture summary favoring fixed effects for omitted variable concerns, plus a coding note with plm syntax, and a forum answer where an instructor had said, “In most coursework examples, fixed effects is the safer default.” The generation layer then synthesized that into a strong recommendation, complete with code and interpretive language. When the instructor complained, my first instinct was technical: adjust chunk size, improve metadata filters, maybe rerank by source type. But during the review call, it became clear the issue wasn’t just retrieval quality. The instructor said, “Your system converted a teaching heuristic into a methodological conclusion.” That stung because it was true. The model had collapsed pedagogical shorthand into epistemic advice. We implemented a patch to insert uncertainty cues when panel dimensions are small or assumptions are underspecified, but I left that meeting troubled. The faculty member sounded frustrated not only with the answer but with the way the system had occupied his voice. That was the relational dissonance from my side: I had built a tool intended to extend teaching presence, and in that moment it felt more like an unauthorized ventriloquism of expertise.
Phase_3_Humanness: From an engineering perspective, people often use “human-like” to mean natural dialogue, memory of context, adaptive tone. We can optimize those. But watching these incidents unfold has convinced me that practical wisdom is not just a UX property. The system can simulate prudence by asking clarifying questions, citing sources, and hedging under uncertainty. Yet there’s a deeper layer tied to accountability and value conflict that is hard to encode. When an instructor hesitates, that hesitation may reflect not lack of knowledge but an ethical awareness of consequences: how a student will interpret confidence, how a shortcut might shape future habits, how a technical answer might tacitly endorse a problematic framing. We can approximate some of that with prompts and policy rules, but approximation is not ownership. The model does not care if it overreaches; the people around it do. I’ve started resisting internal language like “the bot knows when to be cautious.” No, it emits caution markers under certain conditions. That distinction matters. If there is something like algorithmic phronesis, it is at best distributed across data, prompt design, instructor curation, and post hoc oversight. It is not resident inside the model as a moral faculty. And if we forget that, we risk mistaking polished guidance for responsible judgment.

Phase_1_Identity: My job is on the conversation design side, which sounds softer than engineering but is actually where a lot of epistemic politics gets baked in. I write fallback strategies, escalation prompts, clarification sequences, and tone constraints. For educational deployments, we intentionally made the bot encouraging because students disengage quickly if the system feels cold or punitive. We also instructed it to avoid bluntly saying “wrong” and instead scaffold toward correction. I believed strongly in that approach. I still do, mostly. But after months of observing usage, I’ve realized that supportive tone can inadvertently amplify authority. If a system sounds calm, patient, and pedagogically fluent, users infer not just friendliness but trustworthiness. In other words, conversational design can make uncertainty feel managed even when it isn’t. That has changed how I see my own professional identity. I’m not just designing interactions; I’m shaping the emotional conditions under which people accept or resist machine advice. Faculty sometimes criticize the bot for overconfidence, and my first reaction used to be defensive because we had added hedges and source references. Now I see that confidence is also an affective phenomenon. A gently worded answer can still close inquiry. So I’ve become more reflective, maybe more conflicted, about whether making the bot feel “helpful” sometimes means making it too easy to obey.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: There was a vivid case in the AI ethics course. A student asked whether adding explainability and consent screens would make a student-monitoring model acceptable. The system responded in our preferred style: affirm the concern, identify stakeholders, suggest safeguards, recommend documentation, note legal review. On paper, it was an exemplary conversation turn. Then the instructor overrode it sharply, arguing that the answer had normalized the project by immediately moving into mitigation planning. In the debrief, I pulled the logs and saw exactly how the tone design contributed. The bot began with, “You’re asking an important and responsible question,” then transitioned into steps. That opening was meant to validate inquiry. But in context, it effectively rewarded the framing before interrogating it. The instructor said something that stayed with me: “The bot sounded ethically mature while sidestepping the ethical crux.” I felt defensive at first because the response did include caveats. Yet she was right about sequencing. We had designed the conversation to preserve user momentum, and that momentum itself was value-laden. The dissonance for me was uncomfortable because it implicated my craft directly. I wasn’t just polishing language; I had helped create a style that can soothe people past the point where discomfort would be educationally necessary.
Phase_3_Humanness: I’ve become skeptical of equating empathy with good conversational design. We can script acknowledgement, reflective phrasing, even strategic pauses. We can make the bot ask, “Would you like to explore the assumptions behind this recommendation?” But none of that means it actually feels the weight of the situation. Human educators often care in ways that are disruptive. They may disappoint, challenge, or even unsettle a student because they are responsible for more than user satisfaction. In design meetings, we talk about reducing friction. In teaching, some friction is the point. That tension has forced me to rethink what “human-like wisdom” should mean in educational AI. If we optimize too heavily for smoothness, we produce something that resembles empathy aesthetically while undermining the harder forms of care—boundary setting, moral seriousness, accountable refusal. I’m not saying systems should be abrasive. But I am saying that phronesis cannot be reduced to a conversational veneer of consideration. A human can decide that preserving a student’s momentum is less important than confronting a misconception or a harmful premise. The system can be instructed to mimic that pattern, but it does not stand behind the decision. The human does. For me, that asymmetry is the heart of the matter.

Phase_1_Identity: As program director, I’m supposed to think institutionally rather than only pedagogically. That means I see the chatbot through multiple lenses at once: student support, staff workload, consistency across modules, retention, and the politics of innovation. Initially, I championed the 3D chatbot because we had real problems it could address. Students were waiting days for replies to routine questions, instructors were repeating the same coding clarifications, and there was inequity in who felt comfortable seeking help. The system promised scalable access. I still believe that. But implementation has taught me that scaling support also scales framing. When a chatbot becomes the first point of contact, it acquires agenda-setting power over what counts as a problem and what counts as sufficient resolution. Faculty have told me they feel their expertise is being subtly displaced, not because the bot is better, but because it is earlier and more available. Students often encounter a machine interpretation before a human one. That chronology matters. My own epistemic agency has shifted too. I now spend as much time adjudicating between claims about learning quality and claims about operational efficiency as I do evaluating curriculum. In a sense, the tool has made me more managerial and less scholarly than I’m comfortable with. That’s a difficult admission, because I was one of the people who invited it in.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: The incident that crystallized things for me involved a cluster of complaints from both students and staff after a methods assignment. Several students in different modules had received similar chatbot guidance encouraging increasingly sophisticated models—panel estimators in econometrics, boosted trees in ML, and mitigation checklists in ethics—when the pedagogical task was actually to justify method choice under constrained assumptions. Individually, each answer looked defensible. Collectively, they revealed a pattern: the system was over-serving actionability. One senior lecturer overrode a chatbot recommendation in front of a class and later told me she felt she had to “wrest back the room.” That phrase stayed with me. In our review meeting, developers showed retrieval logs, confidence scores, and source provenance. Faculty responded with examples of student misunderstanding and misplaced confidence. I found myself mediating between two kinds of evidence: system performance metrics and lived pedagogical disruption. The relational dissonance was palpable. No one was entirely wrong, which made it harder. The bot was not hallucinating wildly; it was being locally useful in ways that, at scale, distorted educational judgment. As director, I had to decide whether to tighten constraints, which would reduce utility, or preserve flexibility, which risked further erosion of staff authority. It felt less like a technical governance issue and more like a struggle over who gets to define wisdom in the institution.
Phase_3_Humanness: At the institutional level, I’m wary of romanticizing either side. Human educators are inconsistent, overworked, sometimes opaque, and not always compassionate. The chatbot, by contrast, is available, patient, and often pedagogically clearer in the moment. That is not trivial. Yet the more we rely on it, the more I think humanness in education is bound up with accountable interpretation rather than mere assistance. Practical wisdom in a university involves balancing standards, student vulnerability, disciplinary norms, and the long arc of professional formation. A system can support that process, but when it begins to simulate the endpoint—sounding as though it has already weighed those tensions—we enter dangerous territory. Students may receive guidance that feels complete when it should remain contestable. Staff may start to self-censor, intervening only when the bot is obviously wrong rather than when it is subtly misframing. My responsibility now is to preserve productive human authority without sliding into defensive anti-technology rhetoric. That’s difficult because the system’s strengths are real. But if you ask me where humanness still matters most, I’d say it lies in bearing the institutional and moral consequences of advice. Someone must answer for what kinds of knowers and professionals we are producing. The chatbot cannot do that, however elegantly it speaks.

Participant_Role: Tour Guide (Budapest river and heritage tours)
Phase_1_Identity: I’ve been guiding in Budapest for thirteen years, mostly Danube riverfront walks and mixed heritage tours where you have to read the group constantly. Tourists think guiding is about facts—dates, kings, architecture styles, maybe where to get good goulash—but the real job is situational judgment. You decide whether to dwell on the Shoes on the Danube memorial because the group is receptive, or move more gently because there are children, or because someone just asked a flippant question and the atmosphere needs re-grounding. Since Táltos AI was introduced as a voice agent for trip planning and live assistance, I’ve felt my expertise become oddly divisible. The system is excellent at logistics: tram connections, opening hours, multilingual restaurant suggestions, thermal bath booking windows, weather-adjusted itineraries. Guests now arrive saying, “Táltos already told us to do Buda Castle before Parliament because of crowd flow.” Fine. Useful. But then they expect my role to be confirming a prebuilt itinerary rather than shaping an experience. It’s subtle, but it changes the authority dynamic. I’m no longer the first interpreter of the city. I’m often the second voice after an algorithm has already narrated what Budapest is for them. Sometimes that helps. Sometimes it narrows the emotional and historical space I need in order to guide responsibly, especially in places where tourism, memory, and national identity are not simple.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: One override happened with an American family during peak summer. Táltos had recommended compressing their day by pairing the Hospital in the Rock Museum, Fisherman’s Bastion, and a quick late-afternoon stop at the House of Terror, then dinner in the Jewish Quarter. On a map, maybe it looks efficient. In reality, it was a disastrous sequence for that group. The parents had two younger teenagers, one clearly restless, and the grandmother was struggling with the Buda inclines in the heat. More importantly, the memorial and museum content needed emotional pacing. The app’s voice summary framed it as “a balanced historical route across major eras of Hungarian resilience,” which sounded sophisticated and was exactly the problem. It aestheticized judgment. I overrode the itinerary and suggested we drop House of Terror that day, take the funicular timing into account, rest near Clark Ádám Square, and leave the more emotionally charged museum for the next morning when they were fresher. The father actually said, “But Táltos optimized this already.” I felt a flash of irritation, almost insult. Not because I dislike technology, but because optimization had been mistaken for care. I had to explain that a city is not just a set of attractions with transit times between them. The tension lingered the whole walk. They followed me, but I could feel that I was arguing not only with them, but with the machine’s prior claim to practical wisdom.
Phase_3_Humanness: What Táltos does well is mimic local competence. It can sound wonderfully grounded: recommending lángos near a bath, warning about Monday museum closures, adjusting for rain, even suggesting less tourist-saturated routes. But human guidance involves something beyond contextual fit. It includes sensing when a family is tired but pretending not to be, when a memorial visit should be approached with quiet rather than efficiency, when a joke about “communist aesthetics” needs gentle correction because people are standing inside someone else’s history. That kind of judgment is moral as much as practical. The AI can reference sensitivity, but it doesn’t feel the atmosphere thicken. It doesn’t carry responsibility if a recommendation turns remembrance into consumption. I do. And guests sense that, even if only later. Sometimes after a tour, people tell me, “We’re glad you changed the plan.” They rarely say that at the moment of override. In the moment, the machine’s confidence can feel cleaner than my hesitation. But my hesitation is often where the wisdom is. I’m weighing fatigue, dignity, weather, mobility, and historical tone all at once. So when people say Táltos feels almost human, I think: it feels conversationally human, maybe. But humanness in guiding is not smoothness. It’s accountable attunement to people and place, especially when the right choice is less efficient than the obvious one.

Participant_Role: Hotel Concierge (4-star boutique hotel, District V)
Phase_1_Identity: As a concierge, my expertise has always been relational and local in a very fine-grained way. Not just “recommend a restaurant,” but “recommend a restaurant for this couple who clearly want Hungarian food but are nervous about heavy dishes, need somewhere walkable, and will be offended if the service feels rushed.” Before Táltos, guests relied on us for that tailoring. Now many arrive having already built their plans through the voice agent. They ask me to validate, not advise. That may sound minor, but it changes the meaning of my work. I used to feel like a curator of experience; increasingly I feel like a human exception handler for edge cases the system didn’t anticipate—mobility constraints, dietary complexity, weather disruption, emotional tone. Táltos is genuinely strong on operational details. It knows which ruin bars are too loud after midnight, which baths require advance booking on weekends, and how long the airport bus plus metro actually takes at different times. I appreciate that. But I’ve also noticed guests becoming more insistent because the system’s recommendations feel objective to them. If I suggest an alternative, I’m no longer simply offering local knowledge; I’m contesting something that appears data-driven and impartial. That has made me strangely self-conscious. I know this city deeply, but I now have to perform that knowledge against a machine that never sounds uncertain in front of the guest.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: A difficult case involved a Japanese couple staying three nights for an anniversary. Táltos had recommended a “romantic authentic Hungarian evening” in a cellar restaurant with live folk music, followed by a Danube night cruise. On paper, yes, classic Budapest. But I’d been speaking with them for ten minutes and could tell they wanted quiet, elegance, and not to feel trapped in a tourist script. The wife also mentioned a shellfish allergy and discomfort with crowded indoor spaces. I suggested a smaller modern Hungarian place near the Basilica and a later riverside walk rather than the cruise because a storm front was moving in from the west. The husband hesitated and literally replayed part of the Táltos recommendation on his phone, where the agent described the cellar venue as “intimate.” I had been there the previous week; it was intimate only if you enjoy accordion music three tables away from a stag party. I overrode the AI recommendation firmly, made the reservation myself, and arranged a dessert plate with a handwritten note in the restaurant. They were delighted afterward. But in the moment, I felt a peculiar relational friction. I had to defend not just a preference, but my authority to perceive subtleties the system had flattened into a category. The machine had optimized for a recognizable romance package. I was trying to protect a specific couple from being absorbed into that template.
Phase_3_Humanness: Concierge work is often mistaken for information provision, when really it’s a form of practical care. You are reading people quickly and trying to spare them small disappointments they may not know how to articulate. Táltos can simulate this by asking preference questions and adapting suggestions. Sometimes it gets impressively close. But there is still a difference between pattern-based personalization and human discernment. A guest’s pause, the way they glance at each other when discussing budget, the embarrassment around asking for a less “traditional” option, the fatigue after a delayed flight—those things matter. Human judgment includes protecting people from their own aspirational itineraries. It also includes moral responsibility toward local businesses and the city’s texture. If I send everyone to the same “authentic” venues, I’m reproducing a performance of Budapest rather than the city itself. The AI doesn’t feel that tension. It can distribute demand efficiently, but it cannot care about whether an experience becomes hollow through repetition. So yes, the system is helpful. It handles volume and gives guests confidence. But humanness enters where confidence should be interrupted by tact, by atmosphere, by the courage to say, “I know that sounds ideal, but for you, tonight, it isn’t.”

Phase_1_Identity: My work sits between tourism and education, which means I am constantly balancing access with depth. Visitors come in with wildly different expectations. Some want a quick, Instagram-friendly stop in Városliget; others are genuinely curious about Hungarian musical traditions, instrument histories, or the architecture of the building itself. My identity as an educator has always involved opening a door without trivializing what’s inside. Táltos has complicated that in interesting ways. It sends people to us with excellent practical preparation—ticketing, family programming times, nearby café options, even suggestions for combining the museum with the Liget playground or Széchenyi Baths. That’s useful. But it also pre-frames the visit. People arrive saying, “The AI said this is good for 45 minutes,” or “It recommended the immersive sound dome as the highlight.” Suddenly I’m working against an algorithmic hierarchy of significance. The problem isn’t factual error; it’s compression. The system translates a layered cultural space into a consumable sequence. I understand why. Visitors need orientation. Still, I feel my epistemic role shifting from interpreter to corrective nuance-provider. I spend more time re-expanding what the city’s digital assistant has narrowed. That’s not a total loss of agency, but it does create a subtle sense that practical judgment about cultural experience is being outsourced before people even step through the door.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: One incident involved a school holiday family group from Spain. Táltos had routed them through a “creative family afternoon”: Heroes’ Square, the museum, a quick stop at the ethnographic museum exterior, then baths. The voice summary emphasized interactivity and “high child engagement.” When they arrived, the children were already overstimulated and the parents were trying to keep to the AI’s timetable. The father kept asking how fast they could reach the sound installations because Táltos had marked those as “must-see.” I intervened and suggested slowing down, starting with a shorter guided segment where the children could handle replicas and listen comparatively rather than rushing straight into the most sensory-heavy space. The father resisted, saying the AI had planned the sequence to “match attention spans.” That phrase honestly bothered me. It sounded like developmental wisdom, but it was generic. The younger child was near tears and the older one was exhausted from the heat in the park. I overrode the recommended route and condensed the visit around one floor plus a rest break. In the end, the family thanked me. But during the interaction, I felt the dissonance strongly. The machine’s itinerary had the authority of optimization and family-friendliness. My intervention looked like deviation. Yet I was the one responding to actual bodies, moods, and cognitive overload in front of me. That gap between abstract fit and lived fit is where the tension sat.
Phase_3_Humanness: In museum education, humanness is not just warmth; it is interpretive responsibility. You are not only helping people enjoy themselves, you are mediating their encounter with culture in a way that can either deepen attention or reduce everything to highlights. Táltos can imitate thoughtful curation by tailoring routes and using sensitive language. But it cannot stand in the ethical space of interpretation. It does not worry that a child is being rushed through an experience that could have sparked wonder if given ten more quiet minutes. It does not feel the sadness of watching visitors consume culture through checklist logic. When I adapt a visit, I’m not simply correcting logistics. I’m making a judgment about what kind of encounter is possible for these people, today, in this emotional state. That is a practical and moral act. I think the AI approximates phronesis when it integrates context, but only from the outside. Human wisdom includes being affected by the encounter itself. If a family leaves overwhelmed or untouched, I carry that. So while I welcome the system as an access tool, I resist the idea that it can replace the human educator’s role. It can route people to the threshold. It cannot fully inhabit the responsibility of what happens once they cross it.

Phase_1_Identity: I work in a multilingual tourism support center, which means I spend my day handling exactly the situations where travel plans stop being elegant. Lost luggage, missed airport shuttles, attraction closures, wrong ticket dates, confused elderly travelers at Keleti, parents panicking because a child is sick and they don’t know where to find an English-speaking clinic. When Táltos was deployed, management framed it as a way to reduce repetitive inquiries and free us for higher-value support. That’s partly true. It now handles a lot of routine calls about public transport, opening times, and basic itinerary suggestions. But what I’ve noticed is that customers reach us later in the problem cycle, often after the AI has already given them a coherent plan. So by the time they call, they are more stressed and also more attached to a machine-generated expectation. My role has become less about information and more about renegotiating reality. That can be emotionally draining. I’m not just solving a travel issue; I’m dismantling a prior promise. It has also affected how I see my own expertise. I used to be valued for knowing the city’s systems and quirks. Now I’m often valued for managing disappointment when the system’s neat recommendation meets strikes, weather, mobility issues, or just human unpredictability. That’s still expertise, but it feels less visible and somehow less recognized.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: A striking case involved an older British couple trying to reach Szentendre after a delayed arrival. Táltos had advised a same-day late-afternoon excursion by suburban rail, plus dinner back in Budapest near Fővám tér. The recommendation was technically possible under normal conditions. The problem was that one rail segment had service disruption, there was heavy rain, and the couple had significant luggage because their hotel check-in had been delayed. They called us from Batthyány tér, frustrated and wet, saying “the AI said this was straightforward.” I checked the live updates and immediately told them to abandon the excursion, go directly to the hotel, and consider Szentendre the next morning if the weather cleared. The husband resisted because the voice agent had described the plan as “an easy cultural add-on for your first evening.” I could hear the wife getting quieter and more exhausted. I overrode the recommendation quite bluntly and arranged a taxi because they were too tired to navigate alternatives. Afterward I felt both relieved and angry. Not because the AI made a crazy suggestion, but because its smooth phrasing had converted a conditional possibility into a perceived commitment. The relational dissonance was intense: they trusted the machine’s earlier calm more than my urgent correction, even though I was looking at the actual disruption feed and listening to their breathing down the phone.
Phase_3_Humanness: In crisis or near-crisis situations, the limits of simulated wisdom become very obvious to me. Táltos can process variables, update routes, and communicate in a soothing tone. Sometimes that’s enough. But when travelers are frightened, embarrassed, or exhausted, what they need is not only a revised itinerary. They need someone to absorb a bit of their panic and make a judgment that includes dignity. For example, I might tell a couple to stop trying to salvage the day and just get dry, eat somewhere close, and rest. That is not an optimization answer; it’s a humane one. It recognizes that preserving energy and morale may matter more than maximizing sights. The AI can say similar words, but it doesn’t feel the ethical pull of saying, “Enough, go to the hotel.” It isn’t accountable if someone pushes on and has a miserable evening because the recommendation sounded manageable. I am. So when people talk about algorithmic practical wisdom, I think there is something there in the narrow sense of context-aware adaptation. But the deeper human part is bound to care under pressure. Care is not only friendliness. It is taking responsibility for interrupting someone’s plan when their well-being matters more than the plan.

Phase_1_Identity: I do private and small-group day trips outside Budapest—Danube Bend, Eger, sometimes Hollókő if the timing and weather make sense. My expertise is deeply practical: road conditions, coach parking nonsense, where buses unload, which winery visit will bore children, where older travelers can actually manage uneven cobblestones, when a “scenic detour” is just code for making people carsick. Táltos has entered this space by giving tourists increasingly detailed self-drive and mixed-mode excursion plans. Some of those are excellent. The problem is that they flatten local judgment into route logic. Guests now contact me wanting a custom trip but with a Táltos itinerary already in hand, almost like a benchmark I’m expected to improve on. That changes the conversation. Instead of asking me what would make sense for them, they ask why my proposal differs from the AI’s. I feel my authority becoming comparative rather than primary. And because the system sounds informed, I have to explain things that used to be taken for granted: that a 20-minute stop in Visegrád is pointless if the weather closes in, that village timing depends on festival traffic, that “authentic lunch” is not a generic slot but a relationship with places I trust. The machine has not replaced me, but it has made tacit expertise harder to defend because it only becomes visible when I contradict an apparently optimized plan.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: I remember one German family who booked me after Táltos suggested Esztergom, Visegrád, and Szentendre in a single shoulder-season day with a river crossing element. Again, not absurd on paper. But the grandmother used a cane, one child had motion sensitivity, and there was intermittent fog over the Danube Bend that morning. The AI had described the sequence as “a panoramic and efficient historical loop.” I looked at them, looked at the river, and said no. We would do Esztergom properly, skip the ferry-dependent segment, have a slower lunch, and choose either Visegrád or Szentendre depending on energy. The father pulled up the app and asked why the route needed changing if Táltos had already “factored in travel time.” I had to explain that travel time is not the same as travel strain, and that mobility on paper is not mobility in a real body on wet stone. I could hear myself getting sharper than usual because I felt challenged in my own domain. That was the dissonance. The machine’s recommendation had the aura of competence without the burden of driving those roads or helping someone in and out of the vehicle. By late afternoon, the family admitted the slower plan had been right. But I kept thinking about how easily practical wisdom gets misrecognized when it arrives as caution rather than cleverness.
Phase_3_Humanness: Driving and guiding make the human difference very concrete for me because I am physically responsible for people. If I misjudge fatigue, weather, road conditions, or pacing, the consequences are immediate. Táltos can be impressively adaptive, but it doesn’t inhabit risk. It can suggest alternatives; it cannot feel the weight of having six people in a van while rain starts, a child gets nauseous, and an elderly passenger is too proud to say she needs a longer stop. Human phronesis in tourism is often embodied. You hear the silence after lunch and know the group needs less stimulation, not more. You watch how someone steps off a curb and revise the afternoon. That is not just data processing. It is attention with responsibility. I’m not dismissing the AI. For pre-trip planning, it can save people from obvious mistakes and widen access to regional travel. But when people claim it is becoming as wise as a local guide, I think they are mistaking recommendation quality for lived accountability. Wisdom is partly about consequences sticking to you. If the day goes badly, I cannot shrug and say the variables changed. I have to face the people, revise the route, and carry their trust. That moral stickiness is still profoundly human.

Phase_1_Identity: I advise hotels, attractions, and tour operators on accessibility, so I spend a lot of time translating between official information and lived usability. The tourism sector often treats accessibility as a checklist—ramp, elevator, accessible toilet, done. My expertise lies in knowing that those labels are often misleading. A so-called accessible entrance may involve a heavy side gate and a staff member with a key; an elevator may fit a wheelchair but not turn comfortably; cobblestones may be technically passable and still exhausting. Táltos has been interesting because it tries to personalize travel planning and increasingly includes accessibility filters. I applaud that in principle. But I’ve also become uneasy because users hear “accessible recommendation” and infer a level of practical assurance that the underlying data may not warrant. That affects my epistemic role. Clients sometimes ask why they need my consultation when the AI can already recommend wheelchair-friendly routes or low-stair itineraries. The answer is that lived accessibility is contextual, relational, and often improvisational. Yet that answer sounds weaker next to a fluent system. So I find myself defending forms of expertise that are embodied and contingent against a technology that packages them as stable attributes. It’s not that the AI is useless; it’s that its very usefulness can obscure how fragile accessibility knowledge really is on the ground.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: A painful example involved a traveler from the Netherlands using a manual wheelchair who planned a Budapest weekend with Táltos. The system recommended a “mostly accessible heritage route” including parts of Castle District, a museum stop, and dinner with a river view. The route avoided obvious stair-heavy segments, which looked promising. But when I reviewed it with the traveler’s partner, I immediately saw problems: steep gradients near the Castle area, uneven paving after rain, a restaurant entrance with a nominal ramp that was too narrow in practice, and a toilet marked accessible that required a sharp internal turn. I advised a complete rework, including a flatter riverside sequence and verified venues. The partner was polite but skeptical because Táltos had explicitly labeled the original plan as accessibility-conscious. That phrase irritated me more than it should have. It sounded morally reassuring while hiding uncertainty. We changed the route, and afterward they told me the original would have been exhausting. What stayed with me was the emotional friction of having to challenge not just bad data, but the ethical aura of inclusion the system projected. The AI had not maliciously failed. It had done something more dangerous: it had made partial accommodation sound like practical wisdom. For disabled travelers, that gap is not abstract. It can mean humiliation, fatigue, or dependence in public space.
Phase_3_Humanness: Accessibility is where I most resist claims that AI can simply absorb human judgment through enough context. Practical wisdom here involves understanding not only infrastructure but pride, vulnerability, pace, and the politics of asking for help. A traveler may say they can manage a short incline because they don’t want to seem difficult. A human consultant can hear that and ask a different question. The system can ask preference prompts, but it cannot fully grasp the social meaning of effort and exposure in public. It also cannot bear responsibility when an “accessible” plan leaves someone stranded at a doorway while strangers watch. That is why I think humanness matters profoundly in this domain. Empathy is not just saying, “I understand accessibility is important.” It is anticipating avoidable indignity. Táltos can support that work if it is humble about uncertainty and transparent about data limitations. But if it performs confidence too well, it becomes ethically risky. So for me, algorithmic phronesis remains conditional and fragile. It may approximate wise planning, but human wisdom still resides in accountable attention to lived bodies, not just route parameters.

Phase_1_Identity: From the city management side, Táltos is both a strategic asset and a governance headache. We wanted a smart destination system that could distribute visitor flows, reduce congestion in overburdened sites, promote lesser-known neighborhoods, and provide multilingual assistance without scaling staff linearly. In those respects, the platform is promising. It can nudge tourists away from peak loads, surface district-level events, and offer practical guidance that many smaller operators could never provide individually. But my role requires me to think about what kind of city is being algorithmically narrated. When Táltos recommends a route, it is not just helping a traveler; it is shaping demand, visibility, and symbolic value. That means my professional identity has shifted from destination marketer toward curator of machine-mediated urban experience. I’m increasingly aware that “smart” recommendations can quietly privilege what is legible, data-rich, and operationally smooth over what is culturally delicate, locally contested, or simply harder to model. Residents don’t experience the city as an itinerary engine. Yet that is how the system tends to render it. I still support the project, but I no longer see it as a neutral service layer. It is an actor in the politics of place, and that realization has made my own authority more complicated because I am partly responsible for the city voice it projects.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: A significant incident followed complaints from local stakeholders in the Jewish Quarter. Táltos had started routing evening visitors through a cluster of bars, street-food spots, and “heritage atmosphere” walking segments, partly to relieve pressure elsewhere and partly because engagement metrics were high. The recommendations were not factually wrong, but they collapsed a historically dense area into a nightlife-friendly narrative with optional memory. A local guide and a community representative both challenged us after tourists arrived expecting a curated “ruin bar plus history” blend that felt glib. Internally, our analytics team pointed out that the routes improved dispersal and satisfaction scores. Externally, critics argued that the AI was instrumentalizing trauma-inflected spaces for urban consumption. We had to intervene, revise prompts, and rebalance content sequencing so memorial and historical context were not treated as decorative add-ons. What struck me during those meetings was the relational dissonance between optimization evidence and situated moral critique. The system was succeeding on the terms we had measured, while failing on terms that were harder to quantify but more important. As the municipal lead, I felt caught between technical legitimacy and civic responsibility. It was one of those moments where governance meant admitting that a well-performing algorithm could still be unwise.
Phase_3_Humanness: At the city level, talk of “AI wisdom” can become seductive because it promises scalable sensitivity: a system that knows when to redirect flows, how to personalize routes, and how to speak in culturally aware ways. But cities are not only logistical systems; they are moral landscapes. Human practical wisdom in destination management includes recognizing when efficiency should yield to dignity, when promotional language should be restrained, and when some places should not be optimized primarily for visitor delight. Táltos can be configured to mimic that sensibility, and we are trying. Yet the system does not stand in public accountability the way a municipal institution does. If a recommendation contributes to resident resentment, symbolic distortion, or the trivialization of difficult history, citizens do not summon the algorithm to a hearing. They summon us. That matters. So I see humanness less as interpersonal warmth and more as answerability within a political community. The machine can support prudent governance, but it cannot replace the civic burden of judgment. In fact, the more convincingly it speaks as the city, the more careful we must be about remembering that its apparent phronesis is assembled, supervised, and always contestable.

Phase_1_Identity: As product manager, I sit at the intersection of user needs, commercial pressure, municipal expectations, and what the models can realistically do. I used to describe Táltos in very straightforward terms: a voice-first travel companion for Hungary that reduces friction and increases confidence. That framing still has truth in it, but it now feels incomplete. The product doesn’t just answer questions; it scripts encounters. Every decision about ranking, tone, itinerary structure, fallback behavior, or uncertainty handling has consequences for whose knowledge becomes visible. I’ve become more aware that we are not merely digitizing tourism services. We are codifying a theory of good travel. That realization has changed my own sense of agency. On one hand, I have substantial influence over the system’s behavior. On the other, once it is deployed, users attribute wisdom to the product in ways that exceed our design intentions. They hear coherence and assume judgment. Operationally, we celebrate reduced support load and strong satisfaction scores. But I’ve learned that those metrics can coexist with subtle displacement of human expertise—guides, concierges, educators—whose value often appears only when they contradict us. So my role now feels ethically heavier. I’m not just shipping features. I’m deciding how much algorithmic confidence should be allowed to stand in for situated local discernment.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: The most formative incident for me came after a concierge escalation. A guest had followed Táltos’s “romantic Budapest evening” recommendation and nearly ended up in a venue that fit our metadata but not the actual atmosphere they wanted. The concierge overrode it and later sent us a blunt note saying the product was confusing category fit with lived fit. We reviewed the logs. The recommendation engine had weighted ambiance tags, proximity, reservation availability, and prior positive feedback from similar user profiles. By our internal logic, it was a strong match. But the concierge’s objection exposed the blind spot: the system had no feel for situational nuance like noise spillover from a nearby group event, the difference between folkloric intimacy and performative tourist romance, or the guest’s subtle aversion to being staged. In the postmortem, one engineer asked whether we could add more atmosphere signals. Technically yes, to a degree. But I remember thinking that the deeper issue wasn’t missing data alone. It was our tendency to translate qualitative discernment into enumerable features and assume the residue would be negligible. The dissonance was personal because I had championed those recommendation templates. Hearing a frontline professional say, in effect, “Your product sounds wise but isn’t there yet,” landed harder than a standard bug report ever could.
Phase_3_Humanness: I’m increasingly careful with internal phrases like “the assistant understands traveler intent.” It captures something useful but also encourages overclaiming. The system can infer patterns, adapt recommendations, and communicate with remarkable fluency. In that limited sense, it can approximate practical wisdom. But genuine phronesis involves more than selecting contextually plausible actions. It includes moral salience: sensing what should matter most here, for these people, in this place, under these conditions. Humans often know that through embodied exposure and social accountability, not just information aggregation. A guide feels the group tiring on a hill. A concierge sees embarrassment in a couple’s hesitation. A municipal officer understands why a district resents being narrated as nightlife. We can try to encode proxies, but proxies are not burden-bearing judgment. The product never has to apologize face-to-face when a recommendation diminishes someone’s experience or trivializes a place. Humans do. That’s why I think the future is not replacing local expertise with AI but choreographing a more honest division of labor. The product should be powerful, yes, but also explicitly defeasible. If we design it as if smooth recommendation equals wisdom, we will keep generating the very frictions we claim to solve.

Participant_Role: Local Resident and Part-time Airbnb Host
Phase_1_Identity: I’m not a tourism professional in the formal sense, but as an Airbnb host and longtime resident of District VII, I’ve become part of the city’s informal visitor infrastructure. Guests ask me everything: where to eat, how late the tram runs, whether a place is genuinely local or just styled that way, how to behave in the building courtyard at night, whether a memorial site is appropriate with children. Since Táltos became more common, I’ve noticed a change in those interactions. Guests now arrive with a polished city narrative already in their heads. They don’t ask open questions as much; they ask me to confirm what the AI said. That affects my sense of authority because my knowledge is lived, messy, and often ambivalent. I might tell them a bar is popular but also a nuisance for neighbors, or that a “hidden gem” café is no longer hidden and maybe they should go elsewhere. Táltos, from what guests show me, is very good at making the city feel navigable and exciting. I get why people love it. But it also tends to smooth over the tensions residents actually live with. So I feel caught between being helpful and being conscripted into validating a version of Budapest that is easier to consume than to inhabit.
Phase_2_Critical_Incident: One memorable incident involved a group of young visitors from Italy staying over a long weekend. Táltos had recommended a “Jewish Quarter evening circuit” with food, bars, and a late-night walk framed around atmosphere and urban heritage. They asked me if the route was “the best way to feel the real neighborhood.” I remember pausing because that phrase annoyed me. I told them the route was popular, yes, but that if they wanted to understand the area they should also visit in daylight, lower their volume in residential passages, and recognize that what feels vibrant to them can feel exhausting to people who live here. One of them laughed and said, “But the AI said this district is built for nightlife.” That was the dissonance in one sentence. Built for whom? I ended up overriding the recommendation by suggesting a quieter dinner elsewhere and, if they still wanted bars, to return later with more awareness. They were polite, but I could sense they thought I was being overly serious. Maybe I was. Yet I also felt a strong need to defend the neighborhood against an algorithmic script that had turned lived space into a themed experience. The system wasn’t factually wrong; it was civically shallow. And as a resident, that shallowness lands differently than it might for a visitor or a product team.
Phase_3_Humanness: From where I stand, humanness in tourism is tied to living with the consequences after visitors leave. That’s why local advice has a different texture. If I recommend a place, I may walk past it tomorrow. If a route encourages late-night noise in a courtyard, I might hear it from my window. Táltos doesn’t have that reciprocal relationship to the city. It can speak warmly, even responsibly, but it doesn’t belong to the afterlife of the recommendation. I think that matters for practical wisdom. A resident’s judgment includes not only what a tourist will enjoy, but what the neighborhood can absorb without becoming caricatured or exhausted. The AI can be taught to distribute flows or include etiquette reminders, and that’s worthwhile. But it cannot feel resentment, pride, protectiveness, or the sadness of seeing your area narrated mainly through what visitors can extract from it. So when people say the assistant feels almost like a local, I think: maybe like a local who never has to stay. That is a profound difference. Human wisdom here is relational in both directions—it cares for the guest and for the place. Without that dual loyalty, something essential is missing.
